facts.claim: GitHub's guide to creating a new repository says you can create a repository on your personal account or on any organization where you have sufficient permissions, and that you type a name and an optional description.
GitHub's guide to creating a new repository says a repository name must not exceed 100 characters and can only contain ASCII letters, digits, and the characters . , - and _.
GitHub's guide to creating your first repository using GitHub Desktop says GitHub Desktop can be used to create and manage a Git repository without using the command line.
GitHub's guide to committing and reviewing changes in GitHub Desktop says you write a commit message in the Summary field, with an optional Description, and then click Commit to the branch.
GitHub's guide to commits says a commit records changes to one or more files in a branch, with a commit message, and each commit has a unique ID called a SHA or hash.

GitHub's guide to GitHub flow says creating a branch gives you a space to work without affecting the default branch, and that a short, descriptive branch name lets collaborators see ongoing work at a glance.
GitHub's guide to GitHub flow says to make a separate branch for each set of unrelated changes, which makes it easier for reviewers to give feedback.

GitHub's guide to reviewing proposed changes in a pull request says reviewers examine each changed file, leave comments on specific changes, and submit a review that approves the pull request or requests changes.
GitHub's guide to merging a pull request says a repository's rules or branch protection can require reviews or status checks before merging.

GitHub's guide to removing sensitive data says sensitive data can be removed from the history of a repository if you can carefully coordinate with everyone who has cloned it and you are willing to manage the side effects.
GitHub's guide to removing sensitive data says that if the sensitive data is a secret such as a password, token or credential, the first step is to revoke and/or rotate that secret.
GitHub's secret scanning guide says secret scanning scans the entire Git history on all branches of a repository for hardcoded credentials, including API keys, passwords and tokens.
Anthropic lets you set your own monthly spend limit below your tier's cap on the spend limits page, and requests return HTTP 400 once a spend limit you set is reached.
OpenAI's spend-limits guide says a spend alert sends a notification and does not stop traffic, while a hard spend limit makes affected API requests return a 429 error.
GitHub Pages is a static site hosting service that takes HTML, CSS and JavaScript files straight from a repository on GitHub and publishes a website, optionally running them through a build process.
After a push, it can take up to 10 minutes for changes to a GitHub Pages site to publish.
Connecting a Cloudflare Pages project to a GitHub repository makes Cloudflare automatically deploy the code every time a change is pushed to a branch.
Each new branch receives a preview deployment with its own address, and preview deployments do not affect custom domains or the production site.
A rollback instantly reverts a Cloudflare Pages project to a previous production deployment, and preview deployments are not valid rollback targets.
GitHub's guide to READMEs says you can add a README file to your repository to tell other people why your project is useful, what they can do with your project, and how they can use it.
GitHub's guide to READMEs says a README is often the first item a visitor will see when visiting your repository.
GitHub's guide to managing your profile README says you can add a README to your GitHub profile to tell other people about yourself.
GitHub's guide to pinning items to your profile says you can pin gists and repositories to your profile so other people can quickly see your best work.

GitHub's guide to managing teams and people with access to a repository says that for each repository you administer, you can see every team or person with access, invite new people, change each person's role, or remove access.
GitHub's guide to requesting a pull request review says that to request a review you need write access to the repository, and the person you ask receives a notification.

GitHub's guide to protected branches says branch protection rules define whether collaborators can delete or force push to a branch and set requirements for pushes, and lists Require pull request reviews before merging as one option.

GitHub's guide to giving reviews says a comment leaves general feedback without approving or requesting changes, approve signals that the changes are ready to merge, and request changes flags feedback the author should address before merging.
GitHub's guide to merge conflicts says Git cannot safely choose which version of conflicting content to keep, and you must resolve all merge conflicts before you can merge a pull request on GitHub.

GitHub's guide to merge conflicts says simple line conflicts can often be resolved on GitHub, while more complex conflicts must be resolved in a local clone and pushed back to the pull request branch.

GitHub's guide to comparing commits says the repository commit history and a single file's commit history can show different results, because a file's history shows only the commits that affected that file.
A GitHub pull request page has Conversation, Commits, Checks, Files changed and Findings tabs.
GitHub's guide to about commits says each commit has a unique ID called a SHA or hash.
